# Lesson objectives

<!-- Generated by scripts/build_objectives_guide.mjs from the lesson packs. Edit the packs, then run the script; do not edit this page. -->

What each of the 18 lessons is for, and what a learner should be able to do at the end of it. The wording is the instructor's (written 2026-10-12). It lives in the lesson packs, `web/*-lessons.json`, as four fields on each lesson, and this page is generated from them.

| Field | What it holds | Shown to learners |
|---|---|---|
| `purpose` | One sentence: what the lesson is for. | Yes, at the top of the end-of-lesson self-check |
| `coreIdea` | The single thought to leave with, where there is one. | Yes, in the self-check |
| `outcomes` | What a learner should be able to do, one sentence each (a heading and its sentences for a lesson with parts). | Yes: the self-check ticks them off |
| `syllabusNote` | Why the lesson is in the syllabus, in the instructor's words. | No: for authors and reviewers |

## How to use them

- **Writing or reworking a lesson:** read its purpose and outcomes first. Every outcome should be taught in a step, and where it can be tested, asked in one of the lesson's checks. An outcome no step teaches is a gap in the lesson, not in the list.
- **Changing an outcome:** edit it in the pack. A learner's ticks are kept per sentence, so a reworded outcome starts unticked.
- **For learners:** the last screen of each lesson lists the outcomes as a "Check yourself" tick-list. The ticks are saved on the learner's own device and nowhere else.

## The storyline

The order in which the instructor wants the module to read as one story (`data/curriculum-storyline.json`), compared with the order the app uses today.

| # | Step | The question it answers | Lesson | In the app |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | History | Why engines exist | History of Mechanical Engines | Lesson 01 |
| 2 | Aviation context | How aircraft engines evolved | History of Aircraft Engines | Lesson 02 |
| 3 | Language | How we describe them | Terminologies | Lesson 03 |
| 4 | Thermodynamics | Why they can produce work | Thermodynamic Cycles | Lesson 04 |
| 5 | Classification | What forms they take | Classification | Lesson 05 |
| 6 | Cooling | How we keep them cool | Cooling Methods | Lesson 07 (differs) |
| 7 | Construction | What they are made of | Parts and Construction | Lesson 06 (differs) |
| 8 | Valve control | How their mechanisms are coordinated | Valve Operating | Lesson 09 (differs) |
| 9 | Accessory power | What else they drive | Accessories & Drives | Lesson 08 (differs) |
| 10 | Power generation | How fuel ultimately becomes useful propulsive power | Power Generation | Lesson 10 |
| 11 | Breathing | How they breathe | Induction & Exhaust | Lesson 11 |
| 12 | Measurement | How we measure what they do | Performance Calculations | Lesson 12 |
| 13 | Performance | Why performance varies | Factors Affecting Power | Lesson 13 |
| 14 | Design requirements | What makes a good aircraft engine | Engine Requirements | Lesson 14 |
| 15 | Malfunctions | How things go wrong | Operation Malfunctions | Lesson 15 |
| 16 | Maintenance | How AMEs keep them healthy | Maintenance & Servicing | Lesson 16 |
| 17 | Wider aviation | Where else piston aviation can take us | Light Sport Aircraft | Lesson 17 |
| 18 | Practical demonstration | Demonstrate that understanding on a real engine | Practicals | Lesson 18 |

The app's lesson order differs from the storyline for: Cooling Methods (storyline 6, app 7); Parts and Construction (storyline 7, app 6); Valve Operating (storyline 8, app 9); Accessories & Drives (storyline 9, app 8).

## The lessons

### Lesson 01 · History of Mechanical Engines

`history-mechanical-engines` · History & Fundamentals

**Purpose.** Establish the bigger human story into which aircraft piston engines fit.

**Core idea.** Human effort → mechanical power → industrial capability → mobility.

Learners should be able to:

- Explain the general purpose of an engine as a machine for converting available energy into useful mechanical work.
- Describe how humans historically relied on human effort, animal power, wind and water before widespread mechanical engines.
- Outline the broad development of steam engines, internal-combustion engines and later mechanical powerplants.
- Explain how engines transformed agriculture, manufacturing, transport and other industries.
- Compare broadly the use of engines in road, rail, marine and aviation transport.
- Explain why mechanical engines are relatively recent inventions in the longer history of civilisation.
- Appreciate how increasing access to mechanical power changed what human beings could move, manufacture and build.

### Lesson 02 · History of Aircraft Engines

`history-aircraft-engines` · History & Fundamentals

**Purpose.** Show why aviation required a particular kind of engine and how aircraft-engine architecture evolved.

Learners should be able to:

- Outline important attempts at human flight before powered heavier-than-air aircraft.
- Distinguish lighter-than-air and heavier-than-air flight.
- Explain why power-to-weight ratio was one of the critical barriers to early powered flight.
- Describe the significance of sustained, controlled powered flight.
- Outline the historical development of aircraft piston engines.
- Recognise early inline, V-type, rotary, radial and horizontally opposed configurations.
- Explain why different engine arrangements suited different aircraft and periods.
- Explain why radial engines became important in one era of aviation.
- Explain broadly why horizontally opposed engines became common in modern light aircraft.
- Explain why gas-turbine engines eventually replaced very large piston engines in many high-power applications.
- Relate aircraft-engine evolution to changing requirements for power, weight, reliability, cooling, drag and maintainability.

_Syllabus note: This provides historical context for the formal requirement to understand radial, V-type, inline, flat and opposed engine arrangements._

### Lesson 03 · Terminologies

`terminologies` · History & Fundamentals

**Purpose.** Establish the language needed to reason accurately throughout the rest of the module.

Learners should be able to:

- Distinguish aircraft, aeroplane/airplane, airframe, engine and powerplant.
- Distinguish part, component, assembly, mechanism, system and subsystem.
- Define and relate force, work, energy, torque, power and efficiency.
- Distinguish heat from temperature.
- Use basic pressure, volume and temperature terminology correctly.
- Define bore, stroke, swept volume/displacement, TDC, BDC and compression ratio.
- Explain terms such as cycle, stroke, RPM and firing order at an introductory level.
- Distinguish maintenance, servicing, inspection, check, repair and overhaul.
- Use aviation-engine terminology precisely when describing systems and engine operation.

_Syllabus note: This vocabulary prepares students for the module's later requirements involving fuel consumption, engine particulars, power calculations, compression ratio and cylinder volume._

### Lesson 04 · Thermodynamic Cycles

`thermodynamic-cycles` · Fundamentals & Classification

**Purpose.** Explain the scientific principle by which thermal energy can eventually produce mechanical work.

Learners should be able to:

- Explain the concept of a heat engine.
- Explain why thermodynamic cycles are used as simplified models of real engine processes.
- Identify basic thermodynamic processes involving pressure, volume, heat addition and heat rejection.
- Explain the constant-volume process.
- Interpret a simple pressure-volume diagram.
- Describe the ideal Carnot cycle as a conceptual reference for heat-engine efficiency.
- Describe and illustrate the ideal Otto cycle using a P–V diagram.
- Distinguish the theoretical Otto cycle from the practical piston-engine cycle.
- Describe and illustrate the Diesel cycle.
- Differentiate the Diesel cycle from the Otto cycle.
- Explain the basic combustion process of a Diesel engine.
- Explain major limitations of Diesel engines in aircraft applications.
- Recognise the Brayton cycle as the thermodynamic basis of gas-turbine engines.
- Distinguish a thermodynamic cycle from a mechanical operating cycle.
- Compare two-stroke and four-stroke operation.
- Relate crankshaft rotation to piston movement over an operating cycle.
- Recognise that practical valve events do not occur exactly at TDC and BDC.

_Syllabus note: These are directly aligned with the formal Otto and Diesel outcomes in the module description._

### Lesson 05 · Classification

`classification` · Fundamentals & Classification

**Purpose.** Show students that the same engine can be classified in several different ways depending on the characteristic being considered.

Learners should be able to:

- Explain the purpose of classifying aircraft piston engines.
- Classify engines according to cylinder arrangement.
- Recognise inline, V-type, horizontally opposed, radial and historically relevant rotary arrangements.
- Classify engines according to the number of cylinders.
- Explain why individual engine cylinders must be numbered.
- Describe common cylinder-numbering conventions and relate numbering to maintenance, firing order and fault identification.
- Classify engines as air-cooled or liquid-cooled.
- Classify engines as two-stroke or four-stroke.
- Distinguish spark-ignition and compression-ignition engines.
- Distinguish naturally aspirated, supercharged and turbocharged engines.
- Distinguish carburetted and fuel-injected engines.
- Distinguish direct-drive and geared engines.
- Compare broad advantages and disadvantages of the major engine arrangements.

_Syllabus note: Cylinder arrangement, general classification and cylinder numbering are explicitly required in the source curriculum._

### Lesson 06 · Parts and Construction

`parts-construction` · Fundamentals & Classification

**Purpose.** Build a physical understanding of what the piston engine is made from and why its components take the forms they do.

Learners should be able to:

- Identify the principal structural and power-producing components of an aircraft piston engine.
- Identify and state the functions of the crankcase, accessory case and oil sump.
- Identify the crankshaft, connecting rods, pistons and cylinders.
- Explain the basic relationship between piston, connecting rod and crankshaft.
- Identify and explain the purpose of engine bearings.
- Identify and explain the function of engine drive shafts where applicable.
- Distinguish major stationary and moving components.
- Explain the main mechanical and thermal loads experienced by important engine parts.
- Identify common materials used for crankcases, pistons, crankshafts, connecting rods, cylinder heads, cylinder barrels, bearings and valves.
- Explain why different materials are selected for different engine components.
- Identify engine mounts and shock mounts.
- Explain how engine mounts transfer engine loads into the aircraft structure.
- Explain how shock mounts help isolate vibration.
- Relate component design and material selection to strength, mass, wear, heat transfer and maintainability.
- Locate major components on an actual engine, cutaway model or 3D model.

_Syllabus note: This lesson directly covers the construction elements identified in the official syllabus._

### Lesson 07 · Cooling Methods

`cooling-methods` · Fundamentals & Classification

**Purpose.** Explain the apparent paradox that although heat produces engine power, excessive heat must be removed.

Learners should be able to:

- Explain why only part of the energy released by combustion becomes useful mechanical work.
- Explain why an operating piston engine requires continuous heat rejection.
- Describe the consequences of excessive engine temperature.
- Describe the principle of air cooling.
- Identify cooling fins, baffles, cowling and airflow passages.
- Explain how airflow is directed around an air-cooled engine.
- Describe the principle of liquid cooling.
- Identify the principal components of a typical liquid-cooling system.
- Describe the purpose and desirable characteristics of engine coolants.
- Explain why water may be combined with additives or other coolant fluids.
- Compare air and liquid cooling in terms of weight, complexity, temperature control, reliability, drag and maintenance.
- Identify examples of engines that use each cooling method.
- Explain why one cooling method may be selected over another for a particular aircraft application.

_Syllabus note: Cooling methods and design are explicitly required under engine construction._

### Lesson 08 · Accessories & Drives

`accessories-and-drives` · Accessories & Drives

**Purpose.** Show that the crankshaft does much more than simply turn the propeller.

Learners should be able to:

- Explain why an operating aircraft engine requires a range of mechanically driven accessories.
- Trace mechanical power from the crankshaft to the accessory section.
- Identify common engine-driven accessories.
- State the functions of common accessories including magnetos, oil pumps, fuel pumps, tachometer drives and propeller-governor drives.
- Recognise alternators/generators, vacuum pumps and other possible accessory loads.
- Identify components commonly mounted on the accessory housing.
- Explain how an accessory gearbox distributes mechanical power.
- Describe the operation and application of spur gears.
- Describe the operation and application of bevel gears.
- Explain the purpose of a propeller reduction gear and shaft.
- Explain why some engines use reduction gearing while others drive the propeller directly.
- Distinguish wet-sump and dry-sump arrangements.
- Recognise how accessory-drive failure could affect continued engine operation.

_Syllabus note: The formal module explicitly requires propeller reduction gearing, bevel gears, spur gears, wet/dry sump arrangements and accessory-housing components._

### Lesson 09 · Valve Operating

`valve-operating` · Valve Train & Power Generation

**Purpose.** Explain how crankshaft rotation is mechanically coordinated with the opening and closing of the engine valves.

Learners should be able to:

- Explain the purpose of the intake and exhaust valves.
- Explain engine valve action.
- Identify the principal components of the valve-operating mechanism.
- Trace mechanical motion from the crankshaft through the valve train to the valve.
- Explain the relationship between crankshaft and camshaft speed in a four-stroke engine.
- Explain why the camshaft rotates once for every two crankshaft revolutions.
- Explain how gears maintain correct crankshaft-to-camshaft timing.
- Describe the functions of cam lobes, tappets/lifters, pushrods, rocker arms and valve springs.
- Explain valve lead, valve lag and valve overlap.
- Explain why valve lead, lag and overlap can improve engine breathing rather than harm engine performance.
- Interpret a basic valve-timing diagram.
- Describe the operating principle of a hydraulic tappet.
- Compare conventional camshaft arrangements with the cam-ring arrangement used in radial engines.
- Explain why radial-engine geometry requires a different valve-driving arrangement.

_Syllabus note: Valve action, mechanism arrangement, lead, lag, overlap, valve timing and hydraulic-tappet operation are specifically required._

### Lesson 10 · Power Generation

`power-generation` · Valve Train & Power Generation

**Purpose.** Connect the entire energy-conversion chain from fuel to useful aircraft propulsion.

**Core idea.** Chemical energy in fuel → combustion → thermal energy → pressure → piston force → reciprocating movement → crankshaft torque → shaft power → propeller power → thrust.

Learners should be able to:

- Explain the sequence from chemical energy in fuel to thrust, one conversion at a time (see the core idea).
- Explain that hydrocarbon fuel contains stored chemical energy.
- Explain the role of fuel, air and ignition in releasing that energy through combustion.
- Explain how combustion increases gas pressure and temperature inside the cylinder.
- Explain how expanding gases exert force on the piston.
- Explain how the connecting rod and crankshaft convert reciprocating motion into rotation.
- Distinguish force, torque, rotational speed and shaft power.
- Explain that the engine primarily produces shaft power while the propeller converts shaft power into thrust.
- Explain how part of engine output is also consumed in driving engine accessories.
- Recognise how engine mechanical power may indirectly support electrical, hydraulic and pneumatic aircraft services.
- Identify the components forming the piston-engine power-generating assembly.
- State the function of each major power-generation component.
- Define compression ratio and explain its significance to engine operation.
- Explain why combustion events must be correctly distributed among cylinders.
- Define engine firing order.
- Explain why multi-cylinder engines use an arranged firing sequence.
- Explain how firing order contributes to smoother torque delivery, vibration control, cooling distribution and engine operation.
- Relate firing order to cylinder numbering.

_Syllabus note: The official module explicitly requires power-generation assembly components/functions and compression ratio. It also explicitly requires firing order._

### Lesson 11 · Induction & Exhaust

`induction-exhaust` · Breathing & Performance

**Purpose.** Explain how the engine breathes before combustion and disposes of combustion products afterward.

Learners should be able to:

- Trace induction air from the atmosphere to the engine cylinder.
- Explain the purpose of induction filters, ducts and manifolds.
- Explain how induction air is distributed between cylinders.
- Explain why air quantity and air density affect combustion and power.
- Distinguish naturally aspirated and boosted induction systems.
- Explain the basic principle of supercharging.
- Explain the basic principle of turbocharging.
- Explain how exhaust-gas energy can be used to drive a turbocharger.
- Identify the turbine, compressor, wastegate and intercooler where fitted.
- Trace exhaust gases from the cylinder to atmosphere.
- Describe the purpose of an exhaust manifold.
- Explain the general arrangement of an opposed-engine exhaust system.
- Explain the arrangement of a radial-engine exhaust system.
- Describe the functions of exhaust mufflers and heat exchangers.
- Explain how exhaust-system heat may be used for cabin heating.
- Explain exhaust back pressure and its influence on engine operation.
- Recognise the relationship between exhaust and induction behaviour.
- Explain the dangers of exhaust leakage and carbon-monoxide contamination.

_Syllabus note: The source specifically requires exhaust manifolds, radial-engine exhaust arrangements, mufflers/heat exchangers and exhaust back pressure._

### Lesson 12 · Performance Calculations

`performance-calculations` · Breathing & Performance

**Purpose.** Move from qualitative engine understanding to quantitative description.

Learners should be able to:

- Define and distinguish work, torque and power mathematically.
- Perform simple work calculations.
- Relate torque, rotational speed and shaft power.
- Explain the meaning and historical origin of horsepower.
- Convert between horsepower, watts and kilowatts.
- Calculate swept volume from bore and stroke.
- Calculate individual cylinder volume and total engine displacement.
- Calculate or determine compression ratio from cylinder volumes.
- Explain specific fuel consumption.
- Perform introductory fuel-consumption and efficiency calculations.
- Explain engine efficiency as the relationship between useful output and energy input.
- Convert relevant engineering units correctly.
- Check calculated answers for correct units and reasonable magnitude.
- Define engine leading particulars.
- Extract and interpret important data from an engine specification or data sheet.
- Identify leading particulars such as model designation, cylinder arrangement, number of cylinders, bore, stroke, displacement, compression ratio, rated horsepower, rated RPM and firing order.
- Recognise additional specifications such as rotation direction, fuel requirements, oil capacity and other manufacturer data where available.
- Use engine data to compare two different piston engines.

_Syllabus note: The formal module specifically requires specific fuel consumption, leading particulars/data, power calculations, efficiency, compression ratio and cylinder-volume calculation._

### Lesson 13 · Factors Affecting Power

`factors-affecting-power` · Breathing & Performance

**Purpose.** Explain why actual engine output changes even when the engine itself has not fundamentally changed.

Learners should be able to:

- Explain how available oxygen affects combustion and engine output.
- Explain the effect of altitude on air density and naturally aspirated engine power.
- Explain the effect of ambient temperature on engine performance.
- Explain the effect of humidity.
- Explain the concept of density altitude.
- Predict the effect of a hot, high-altitude operating environment on available power.
- Explain how mixture strength affects combustion and engine power.
- Explain why mixture adjustment may be required as altitude changes.
- Explain the influence of manifold pressure.
- Explain the influence of RPM.
- Explain how induction restrictions reduce power.
- Explain the effect of carburettor heat on induction-air density and available power.
- Explain how engine temperature and cooling condition can influence performance.
- Explain how supercharging or turbocharging can compensate for altitude-related loss of induction pressure.
- Predict qualitatively whether a given operating or atmospheric change will increase or reduce engine performance.

_Syllabus note: The official description explicitly requires identification of factors affecting power output and performance._

### Lesson 14 · Engine Requirements

`engine-requirements` · Requirements & Malfunctions

**Purpose.** Move beyond “How much horsepower does it make?” to “What makes this an appropriate aircraft engine?”

Learners should be able to:

- Explain why maximum power alone does not determine the suitability of an aircraft engine.
- Explain the importance of power-to-weight ratio.
- Discuss the importance of reliability and dependability.
- Explain the significance of good fuel economy and specific fuel consumption.
- Explain why engine mass and physical size matter to aircraft design.
- Explain the significance of frontal area and aerodynamic installation.
- Discuss requirements for adequate engine cooling.
- Explain the importance of smooth operation and vibration control.
- Discuss durability and expected service life.
- Explain why ease of inspection, servicing and maintenance is important.
- Discuss operating flexibility over different speeds, loads and atmospheric conditions.
- Explain the importance of simplicity where it improves reliability.
- Discuss redundancy where appropriate to aircraft-engine safety.
- Explain general methods by which reciprocating-engine efficiency may be improved.
- Compare the engine requirements of different aircraft types or missions.
- Evaluate whether a particular engine would be appropriate for a specified aircraft application.

_Syllabus note: Engine efficiency, methods of improvement and reciprocating-engine requirements are explicitly named in the module._

### Lesson 15 · Operation Malfunctions

`operation-malfunctions` · Requirements & Malfunctions

**Purpose.** Teach learners to reason from abnormal engine behaviour back toward possible causes.

Learners should be able to:

- Distinguish normal and abnormal engine operation.
- Explain detonation and describe its likely causes and consequences.
- Explain pre-ignition.
- Distinguish pre-ignition from detonation.
- Explain backfiring.
- Explain afterfiring.
- Explain engine blow-by.
- Relate blow-by to sealing between the piston rings and cylinder.
- Recognise common symptoms of misfiring and rough running.
- Relate excessively rich or lean mixture conditions to abnormal engine behaviour.
- Recognise indications of overheating.
- Recognise introductory signs of lubrication-related problems.
- Relate low compression to possible internal engine defects.
- Recognise abnormal vibration, noise, temperature, pressure or power loss as evidence requiring investigation.
- Develop a basic diagnostic sequence of symptom → possible cause → effect → appropriate further inspection.

_Syllabus note: Backfiring, afterfiring, detonation, pre-ignition and blow-by are specifically identified in the official module description._

### Lesson 16 · Maintenance & Servicing

`maintenance-servicing` · Maintenance, LSA & Practicals

**Purpose.** Explain how engineers preserve the engine's performance, reliability and airworthiness.

Learners should be able to:

- Explain the purpose of aircraft piston-engine maintenance.
- Distinguish servicing, inspection, maintenance, troubleshooting, repair and overhaul.
- Distinguish scheduled from unscheduled maintenance.
- Explain why aircraft maintenance must follow appropriate manufacturer and approved maintenance data.
- Explain the importance of prescribed limits and tolerances.
- Describe common external engine inspection activities.
- Identify evidence of leaks, corrosion, wear, overheating, looseness and physical damage.
- Explain the purpose of engine compression testing.
- Explain the maintenance importance of engine oil, oil filters and screens.
- Describe introductory principles of spark-plug servicing.
- Explain the purpose of valve-train inspection.
- Explain why hydraulic tappets require correct condition and servicing.
- Explain the importance of valve-spring condition.
- Explain why exhaust systems require regular inspection and maintenance.
- Explain the importance of correct fluid servicing.
- Explain why maintenance actions must be correctly recorded.
- Relate preventive maintenance to continued engine reliability and airworthiness.

_Syllabus note: The corresponding practical competencies are completed in Lesson 18 rather than treated as theory only._

### Lesson 17 · Light Sport Aircraft

`light-sport-aircraft` · Maintenance, LSA & Practicals

**Purpose.** Give students a glimpse of the wider world of piston-powered aviation and introduce regulatory awareness.

Learners should be able to:

- Explain broadly what is meant by light-sport and recreational aircraft.
- Recognise that light aircraft may employ engines and installation philosophies different from conventional certified training aircraft.
- Identify representative engines used in light and recreational aircraft.
- Compare broad characteristics such as engine mass, cooling method, operating RPM, gearing and installation.
- Explain why some light-aircraft engines operate at significantly different RPM ranges from conventional direct-drive aircraft engines.
- Appreciate the role of piston engines in recreational flying, sport aviation, experimental aircraft and aircraft ownership.
- Recognise that aircraft category and regulatory status can affect permissible maintenance activity.
- Explain why an engineer must determine the applicable regulatory framework and maintenance privileges before carrying out maintenance.
- Recognise that maintenance privileges may differ between conventional certified aircraft and some recreational/light-aircraft categories.

_Syllabus note: This is enrichment rather than a requirement explicitly stated in the supplied AMT 4212G description, so the regulatory material should ultimately be anchored to the applicable Tanzanian/TCAA framework rather than assumed from another jurisdiction._

### Lesson 18 · Practicals

`practicals` · Maintenance, LSA & Practicals

**Purpose.** Demonstrate whether the conceptual knowledge from Lessons 1–17 can actually be recognised and applied physically.

Learners should be able to:

**Practical A — Demonstration of Piston-Engine Operation**

Using the motorised cutaway engine.

- Identify TDC and BDC.
- Demonstrate intake, compression, power and exhaust strokes.
- Relate piston movement to crankshaft rotation.
- Explain crankshaft-to-camshaft speed relationship.
- Observe and explain valve opening and closing.
- Demonstrate valve timing.
- Identify lead, lag and overlap where visible on the trainer.
- Explain the sequence of energy conversion from combustion pressure to crankshaft rotation.
- Explain how firing events in multiple cylinders combine to produce smoother engine rotation.
- Explain the complete operation of a four-stroke reciprocating engine while manipulating or observing the training engine.

**Practical B — External & Internal Component Identification and Condition**

The emphasis: identify it → state its function → describe its construction → recognise abnormal condition.

- Identify principal externally visible engine components.
- State the function of each identified component.
- Identify the crankcase, accessory case and sump.
- Identify engine mounts and shock mounts.
- Locate induction, exhaust, ignition, lubrication and accessory interfaces.
- Identify representative internal components from dismantled or sectioned assemblies.
- Identify pistons, rings, piston pins, connecting rods, crankshaft, bearings, cylinders and valves.
- Identify representative valve-train components.
- Distinguish major materials and construction features where visible.
- Recognise obvious leakage, corrosion, cracks, wear, scoring, overheating, deposits and physical damage.
- Relate an observed defect to the likely function of the affected component.

**Practical C — Engine Maintenance Procedures**

- Safely dismantle/disassemble a selected piston-engine power-generation assembly.
- Identify components as they are removed.
- Inspect representative components for obvious condition and serviceability.
- Reassemble the selected power-generation assembly in the correct relationship.
- Demonstrate or perform appropriate hydraulic-tappet servicing.
- Inspect valve-train components for corrosion and wear.
- Perform or demonstrate a valve-spring compression check using appropriate training equipment.
- Inspect representative exhaust-system components.
- Identify cracks, leakage, deterioration and attachment problems in an exhaust system.
- Demonstrate appropriate periodic exhaust-system maintenance/inspection.
- Follow appropriate workshop practices, tools and maintenance information while performing practical tasks.

_Syllabus note: The module itself states that workshop practices should be used to develop understanding and specifically identifies engine parts and a piston-engine trainer among the intended learning materials; the lesson is formalised as three practical exercises. They are particularly important because the official module does not stop at theoretical understanding: it explicitly requires students to dismantle and reassemble power-generation assemblies, service hydraulic tappets, inspect valve-train components and check valve-spring compression. It also requires periodic exhaust-system maintenance._
